<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
<meta charset="UTF-8">
<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1">
<title>ASAF Ebook Export — June 09, 2026</title>
<style>
    /* ── Docs view layout ──────────────────────────────────── */
    .docs-view-layout {
        display: flex;
        height: 100%;
        overflow: hidden;
    }
    :root { --docs-nav-w: 220px; }
    .docs-view-nav {
        width: var(--docs-nav-w);
        min-width: var(--docs-nav-w);
        max-width: var(--docs-nav-w);
        flex-basis: var(--docs-nav-w);
        flex-shrink: 0;
        flex-grow: 0;
        background: var(--bg-secondary);
        border-right: none;
        display: flex;
        flex-direction: column;
        overflow: hidden;
    }
    .docs-view-resize-handle {
        width: 5px;
        flex-shrink: 0;
        background: var(--border-color);
        cursor: ew-resize;
        transition: background 0.15s;
        position: relative;
        z-index: 10;
    }
    .docs-view-resize-handle:hover, .docs-view-resize-handle.dragging { background: rgba(99,102,241,0.7); }
    .docs-view-nav-header {
        padding: 14px 14px 10px;
        font-size: 11px;
        font-weight: 600;
        text-transform: uppercase;
        letter-spacing: .06em;
        color: var(--text-secondary);
        border-bottom: 1px solid var(--border-color);
        white-space: nowrap;
        overflow: hidden;
        text-overflow: ellipsis;
    }
    .docs-view-nav-list {
        list-style: none;
        margin: 0;
        padding: 6px 0;
        overflow-y: auto;
        flex: 1;
    }
    .docs-nav-btn {
        display: block;
        width: 100%;
        background: transparent;
        border: none;
        text-align: left;
        padding: 8px 14px;
        font-size: 12px;
        color: var(--text-secondary);
        cursor: pointer;
        border-radius: 4px;
        white-space: nowrap;
        overflow: hidden;
        text-overflow: ellipsis;
    }
    .docs-nav-btn:hover { background: rgba(255,255,255,0.06); color: var(--text-primary); }
    .docs-nav-btn.active { color: var(--color-primary, #0078d4); background: rgba(0,120,212,0.1); font-weight: 600; }
    .docs-view-body {
        flex: 1;
        overflow-y: auto;
        padding: 28px 36px;
    }
    .docs-view-loading {
        color: var(--text-secondary);
        font-size: 14px;
        padding: 40px 0;
    }
    .docs-tab-content { display: none; }
    .docs-tab-content.active { display: block; }
    .docs-section-title {
        font-size: 20px;
        font-weight: 700;
        margin: 0 0 18px;
        padding-bottom: 10px;
        border-bottom: 1px solid var(--border-color);
    }
    .docs-heading { font-size: 15px; font-weight: 600; margin: 18px 0 8px; color: var(--text-primary); }
    .docs-text { font-size: 13px; line-height: 1.7; margin: 0 0 10px; color: var(--text-secondary); }
    .docs-list { font-size: 13px; line-height: 1.7; margin: 0 0 12px 18px; color: var(--text-secondary); }
    .docs-list li { margin-bottom: 4px; }
    .docs-table-wrap { overflow-x: auto; margin: 12px 0 18px; }
    .docs-table { border-collapse: collapse; font-size: 12px; min-width: 100%; }
    .docs-table th { background: var(--bg-secondary); padding: 7px 12px; text-align: left; font-weight: 600; border-bottom: 2px solid var(--border-color); white-space: nowrap; }
    .docs-table td { padding: 6px 12px; border-bottom: 1px solid var(--border-color); vertical-align: top; }
    .docs-table tr:nth-child(even) td { background: rgba(255,255,255,0.02); }
    .docs-code { background: var(--bg-secondary); border: 1px solid var(--border-color); border-radius: 5px; padding: 12px 16px; font-size: 11px; line-height: 1.6; overflow-x: auto; margin: 10px 0 16px; white-space: pre; }
    .docs-mermaid-wrap { margin: 16px 0 24px; min-height: 60px; background: rgba(0,0,0,0.15); border-radius: 6px; padding: 16px; overflow-x: auto; }
    .docs-mermaid-wrap svg { max-width: 100%; height: auto; display: block; margin: 0 auto; }
    .docs-mermaid-error { color: var(--text-secondary); font-size: 11px; }

    /* ── ASAF Ebook typography mode ──────────────────────────────── */
    .ebook-mode .docs-view-body { background: var(--bg-primary); }
    .ebook-mode .docs-tab-content { max-width: 760px; margin: 0 auto; padding-bottom: 80px; }

    /* Chapter header — eyebrow label + large title + accent bar */
    .docs-chapter-header { margin: 0 0 44px; padding: 28px 0 24px; border-bottom: 1px solid rgba(255,255,255,0.09); }
    .docs-chapter-eyebrow { display: block; font-size: 11px; font-weight: 700; letter-spacing: 0.14em; text-transform: uppercase; color: rgba(129,140,248,0.9); margin-bottom: 10px; }
    .ebook-mode .docs-chapter-title { font-size: 30px; font-weight: 800; letter-spacing: -0.022em; line-height: 1.18; color: var(--text-primary); margin: 0 0 18px; }
    .docs-chapter-accent { display: block; width: 42px; height: 3px; background: linear-gradient(90deg, rgba(99,102,241,0.9) 0%, rgba(59,130,246,0.35) 100%); border-radius: 2px; }

    /* Nav: indigo left-border active indicator + full text wrapping */
    .ebook-mode .docs-nav-btn { border-left: 2px solid transparent; transition: background 0.12s, color 0.12s, border-color 0.12s; white-space: normal; overflow: visible; text-overflow: clip; line-height: 1.4; }
    .ebook-mode .docs-nav-btn.active { color: rgba(165,180,252,0.95); background: rgba(99,102,241,0.13); border-left-color: rgba(99,102,241,0.7); font-weight: 600; }
    .ebook-mode .docs-nav-btn:hover:not(.active) { background: rgba(255,255,255,0.04); }

    /* H3 — section heading with left accent bar */
    .ebook-mode .docs-markdown h3.docs-heading { font-size: 20px; font-weight: 700; margin: 50px 0 14px; color: var(--text-primary); padding: 2px 0 2px 14px; border-left: 3px solid rgba(99,102,241,0.65); line-height: 1.3; }
    /* H4 — labelled sub-section eyebrow */
    .ebook-mode .docs-markdown h4.docs-heading { font-size: 12px; font-weight: 700; margin: 32px 0 10px; color: rgba(165,180,252,0.85); text-transform: uppercase; letter-spacing: 0.09em; }
    /* H5 / H6 */
    .ebook-mode .docs-markdown h5.docs-heading { font-size: 12px; font-weight: 600; margin: 22px 0 8px; color: var(--text-secondary); text-transform: uppercase; letter-spacing: .06em; opacity: 0.65; }
    .ebook-mode .docs-markdown h6.docs-heading { font-size: 12px; font-weight: 600; margin: 14px 0 6px; color: var(--text-secondary); }

    /* Body text */
    .ebook-mode .docs-markdown .docs-text { font-size: 15px; line-height: 1.92; margin: 0 0 18px; color: var(--text-secondary); }
    .ebook-mode .docs-markdown .docs-list { font-size: 15px; line-height: 1.82; margin: 0 0 18px 4px; color: var(--text-secondary); padding-left: 22px; }
    .ebook-mode .docs-markdown .docs-list li { margin-bottom: 9px; padding-left: 4px; }
    .ebook-mode .docs-markdown .docs-list li::marker { color: rgba(99,102,241,0.65); }
    .ebook-mode .docs-markdown .docs-list-ordered li::marker { color: rgba(99,102,241,0.65); font-weight: 700; }
    .ebook-mode .docs-markdown strong { color: var(--text-primary); font-weight: 700; }
    .ebook-mode .docs-markdown em { color: rgba(199,210,254,0.78); font-style: italic; }
    .ebook-mode .docs-markdown code { background: rgba(99,102,241,0.11); border: 1px solid rgba(99,102,241,0.22); border-radius: 3px; padding: 1px 6px; font-size: 13px; color: rgba(165,180,252,0.92); font-family: 'Consolas','Monaco',monospace; }

    /* Horizontal rule */
    .ebook-mode .docs-markdown .docs-rule { border: none; border-top: 1px solid rgba(255,255,255,0.07); margin: 44px 0; }

    /* Blockquote / principle callout */
    .ebook-mode .docs-markdown blockquote.docs-blockquote { border-left: 4px solid rgba(129,140,248,0.7); margin: 26px 0; padding: 16px 22px; background: linear-gradient(135deg, rgba(99,102,241,0.1) 0%, rgba(99,102,241,0.04) 100%); border-radius: 0 8px 8px 0; font-style: italic; font-size: 15px; line-height: 1.78; color: rgba(199,210,254,0.88); }

    /* Table — gradient header, clean rows, rounded container */
    .ebook-mode .docs-markdown .docs-table-wrap { margin: 26px 0 34px; border-radius: 8px; overflow: hidden; border: 1px solid rgba(255,255,255,0.09); box-shadow: 0 2px 12px rgba(0,0,0,0.25); }
    .ebook-mode .docs-markdown .docs-table { font-size: 13.5px; width: 100%; border-collapse: collapse; }
    .ebook-mode .docs-markdown .docs-table th { background: linear-gradient(135deg, rgba(99,102,241,0.24) 0%, rgba(59,130,246,0.14) 100%); font-size: 11px; text-transform: uppercase; letter-spacing: .08em; padding: 11px 16px; color: rgba(199,210,254,0.92); font-weight: 700; border-bottom: 1px solid rgba(99,102,241,0.3); white-space: nowrap; }
    .ebook-mode .docs-markdown .docs-table td { padding: 11px 16px; font-size: 13.5px; line-height: 1.58; border-bottom: 1px solid rgba(255,255,255,0.05); vertical-align: top; }
    .ebook-mode .docs-markdown .docs-table tbody tr:hover td { background: rgba(255,255,255,0.025); transition: background 0.1s; }
    .ebook-mode .docs-markdown .docs-table tbody tr:last-child td { border-bottom: none; }

    /* Viz block — card style */
    .ebook-mode .docs-asaf-viz { background: linear-gradient(145deg, rgba(15,23,42,0.88) 0%, rgba(30,41,59,0.52) 100%); border: 1px solid rgba(255,255,255,0.1); border-radius: 12px; padding: 20px 18px 14px; margin: 8px 0 34px; box-shadow: 0 4px 18px rgba(0,0,0,0.3); }

    /* ── ASAF dimension visualization ────────────────────────────── */
    .docs-asaf-viz { margin: 8px 0 20px; background: rgba(0,0,0,0.18); border: 1px solid rgba(255,255,255,0.07); border-radius: 10px; padding: 14px 12px 10px; overflow: hidden; }
    .docs-asaf-viz-label { font-size: 10px; font-weight: 700; text-transform: uppercase; letter-spacing: .08em; color: var(--text-secondary); margin: 0 0 6px; opacity: .65; }
    .docs-asaf-viz-subtitle { font-size: 12px; color: var(--text-secondary); margin: 0 0 10px; opacity: .75; }
    .docs-asaf-viz-body { display: flex; gap: 12px; align-items: flex-start; }
    .docs-asaf-viz-svg-wrap { flex: 1; min-width: 0; }
    .docs-asaf-viz-key { flex-shrink: 0; width: 170px; display: flex; flex-direction: column; gap: 4px; padding-top: 4px; }
    .docs-asaf-viz-key-row { display: flex; align-items: center; gap: 5px; }
    .docs-asaf-viz-key-badge { font-size: 9px; font-weight: 700; padding: 1px 5px; border-radius: 4px; color: #0f172a; letter-spacing: 0.04em; flex-shrink: 0; min-width: 30px; text-align: center; }
    .docs-asaf-viz-key-name { font-size: 9px; color: var(--text-secondary); opacity: 0.7; line-height: 1.25; }
    .docs-asaf-viz-tags { display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; gap: 5px; margin: 10px 0 2px; }
    .docs-asaf-viz-tag { font-size: 11px; padding: 3px 9px; border-radius: 12px; background: rgba(59,130,246,0.1); border: 1px solid rgba(59,130,246,0.22); color: rgba(147,197,253,0.8); white-space: nowrap; }
    .docs-asaf-viz-legend { display: flex; gap: 16px; margin: 8px 0 0; font-size: 10px; color: var(--text-secondary); opacity: .7; flex-wrap: wrap; }
    .docs-asaf-viz-legend-item { display: flex; align-items: center; gap: 5px; }
    .docs-asaf-viz-legend-line { width: 22px; height: 2px; display: inline-block; border-radius: 1px; }

    /* ── Worksheet Wizard ──────────────────────────────────────── */
    .ws-wizard { margin: 0; }
    /* Progress bar */
    .ws-progress { display: flex; align-items: flex-start; gap: 0; margin: 0 0 26px; padding: 14px 18px; background: rgba(0,0,0,0.22); border-radius: 10px; border: 1px solid rgba(255,255,255,0.08); flex-wrap: nowrap; overflow-x: auto; }
    .ws-progress-step { display: flex; flex-direction: column; align-items: center; gap: 4px; min-width: 62px; cursor: default; }
    .ws-progress-step-done { cursor: pointer; opacity: 0.7; }
    .ws-progress-step-done:hover { opacity: 1; }
    .ws-progress-dot { width: 26px; height: 26px; border-radius: 50%; border: 1.5px solid rgba(255,255,255,0.2); display: flex; align-items: center; justify-content: center; font-size: 10px; font-weight: 700; color: var(--text-secondary); background: rgba(255,255,255,0.04); flex-shrink: 0; }
    .ws-progress-step-active .ws-progress-dot { background: rgba(99,102,241,0.85); border-color: rgba(129,140,248,0.9); color: #fff; }
    .ws-progress-step-done .ws-progress-dot { background: rgba(52,211,153,0.2); border-color: rgba(52,211,153,0.55); color: rgba(52,211,153,0.9); }
    .ws-progress-label { font-size: 9px; text-transform: uppercase; letter-spacing: .06em; color: var(--text-secondary); opacity: .6; white-space: nowrap; }
    .ws-progress-step-active .ws-progress-label { color: rgba(165,180,252,0.9); opacity: 1; }
    .ws-progress-line { flex: 1; height: 1px; background: rgba(255,255,255,0.1); align-self: flex-start; margin-top: 12px; min-width: 10px; }
    .ws-progress-line-done { background: rgba(52,211,153,0.35); }
    /* Panel */
    .ws-panel { }
    .ws-step-body { }
    .ws-step-title { font-size: 18px; font-weight: 700; color: var(--text-primary); margin: 0 0 8px; }
    .ws-step-desc { font-size: 13px; color: var(--text-secondary); margin: 0 0 22px; line-height: 1.6; }
    /* Form grid */
    .ws-form-grid { display: grid; grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr; gap: 14px 20px; margin: 0 0 24px; }
    .ws-field { display: flex; flex-direction: column; gap: 5px; }
    .ws-field-wide { grid-column: 1 / -1; }
    .ws-label { font-size: 11px; font-weight: 700; text-transform: uppercase; letter-spacing: .07em; color: var(--text-secondary); opacity: .85; }
    .ws-req { color: rgba(251,113,133,0.9); }
    .ws-input { background: rgba(255,255,255,0.05); border: 1px solid rgba(255,255,255,0.12); border-radius: 6px; padding: 8px 12px; font-size: 13px; color: var(--text-primary); outline: none; font-family: inherit; transition: border-color .15s, background .15s; width: 100%; box-sizing: border-box; }
    .ws-input:focus { border-color: rgba(99,102,241,0.65); background: rgba(99,102,241,0.06); }
    .ws-input-sm { font-size: 12px; padding: 5px 10px; }
    .ws-textarea { background: rgba(255,255,255,0.05); border: 1px solid rgba(255,255,255,0.12); border-radius: 6px; padding: 8px 12px; font-size: 13px; color: var(--text-primary); outline: none; font-family: inherit; resize: vertical; transition: border-color .15s, background .15s; width: 100%; box-sizing: border-box; }
    .ws-textarea:focus { border-color: rgba(99,102,241,0.65); background: rgba(99,102,241,0.06); }
    .ws-textarea-sm { font-size: 12px; }
    .ws-select { background: rgba(255,255,255,0.05); border: 1px solid rgba(255,255,255,0.12); border-radius: 6px; padding: 8px 12px; font-size: 13px; color: var(--text-primary); outline: none; font-family: inherit; cursor: pointer; width: 100%; box-sizing: border-box; }
    .ws-select:focus { border-color: rgba(99,102,241,0.65); }
    /* Buttons */
    .ws-btn { padding: 9px 18px; border-radius: 7px; border: none; font-size: 13px; font-weight: 600; cursor: pointer; font-family: inherit; transition: opacity .15s, background .15s; white-space: nowrap; }
    .ws-btn-primary { background: linear-gradient(135deg, rgba(99,102,241,0.9) 0%, rgba(59,130,246,0.85) 100%); color: #fff; }
    .ws-btn-primary:hover { opacity: .88; }
    .ws-btn-secondary { background: rgba(255,255,255,0.07); border: 1px solid rgba(255,255,255,0.14); color: var(--text-primary); }
    .ws-btn-secondary:hover { background: rgba(255,255,255,0.12); }
    .ws-btn-save { background: linear-gradient(135deg, rgba(52,211,153,0.9) 0%, rgba(16,185,129,0.85) 100%); color: #0f172a; font-weight: 700; }
    .ws-btn-error { background: rgba(239,68,68,0.45) !important; color: #fff !important; }
    .ws-btn-success { background: linear-gradient(135deg, rgba(52,211,153,0.9) 0%, rgba(16,185,129,0.85) 100%) !important; color: #0f172a !important; }
    .ws-btn:disabled { opacity: .6; cursor: default; }
    .ws-export-link { display: inline-flex; align-items: center; text-decoration: none; }
    .ws-nav-row { display: flex; align-items: center; gap: 10px; margin-top: 28px; padding-top: 20px; border-top: 1px solid rgba(255,255,255,0.07); }
    .ws-nav-spacer { flex: 1; }
    /* Score slider */
    .ws-slider-wrap { margin: 0 0 20px; }
    .ws-slider-label { font-size: 11px; font-weight: 700; text-transform: uppercase; letter-spacing: .07em; color: var(--text-secondary); opacity: .85; margin-bottom: 10px; }
    .ws-stage-row { display: flex; gap: 4px; margin-bottom: 8px; }
    .ws-stage-cell { flex: 1; display: flex; flex-direction: column; align-items: center; gap: 1px; padding: 5px 2px; border-radius: 5px; border: 1px solid rgba(255,255,255,0.08); transition: all .15s; }
    .ws-stage-num { font-size: 13px; font-weight: 800; color: var(--text-secondary); }
    .ws-stage-lbl { font-size: 7.5px; text-transform: uppercase; letter-spacing: .04em; color: var(--text-secondary); opacity: .55; }
    .ws-stage-cell-active .ws-stage-num { font-size: 15px; }
    .ws-stage-cell-active .ws-stage-lbl { opacity: 1; }
    .ws-slider { -webkit-appearance: none; width: 100%; height: 5px; background: rgba(255,255,255,0.1); border-radius: 3px; outline: none; margin: 4px 0 6px; cursor: pointer; }
    .ws-slider::-webkit-slider-thumb { -webkit-appearance: none; width: 18px; height: 18px; border-radius: 50%; background: rgba(99,102,241,0.9); cursor: pointer; border: 2px solid rgba(255,255,255,0.75); }
    .ws-slider::-moz-range-thumb { width: 18px; height: 18px; border-radius: 50%; background: rgba(99,102,241,0.9); cursor: pointer; border: 2px solid rgba(255,255,255,0.75); box-sizing: border-box; }
    .ws-stage-desc { font-size: 12px; font-style: italic; min-height: 18px; margin-top: 2px; }
    /* Dimension navigator */
    .ws-dim-nav { display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; gap: 5px; margin-bottom: 14px; }
    .ws-dim-dot { padding: 4px 9px; border-radius: 5px; border: 1.5px solid rgba(255,255,255,0.14); background: rgba(255,255,255,0.04); font-size: 10px; font-weight: 700; color: var(--text-secondary); cursor: pointer; transition: all .15s; letter-spacing: .05em; }
    .ws-dim-dot:hover { background: rgba(255,255,255,0.08); }
    .ws-dim-dot-active { border-color: var(--plane-color, rgba(99,102,241,0.7)); background: rgba(99,102,241,0.15); color: var(--text-primary); }
    .ws-dim-dot-done::after { content: '✓'; font-size: 8px; margin-left: 3px; opacity: .7; }
    /* Dimension card */
    .ws-dim-card { border-radius: 10px; border: 1px solid rgba(255,255,255,0.1); overflow: hidden; }
    .ws-dim-header { padding: 14px 16px 12px; border-bottom: 1px solid rgba(255,255,255,0.07); }
    .ws-dim-header-top { display: flex; justify-content: space-between; align-items: center; margin-bottom: 8px; }
    .ws-plane-badge { font-size: 10px; font-weight: 700; letter-spacing: .1em; text-transform: uppercase; }
    .ws-dim-progress { font-size: 11px; color: var(--text-secondary); opacity: .55; }
    .ws-dim-title { font-size: 15px; font-weight: 700; margin: 0 0 6px; color: var(--text-primary); }
    .ws-dim-desc { font-size: 12px; color: var(--text-secondary); line-height: 1.55; margin: 0; opacity: .85; }
    .ws-dim-body { padding: 16px; display: flex; flex-direction: column; gap: 0; }
    /* Summary */
    .ws-stat-chips { display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(4,1fr); gap: 10px; margin-bottom: 18px; }
    .ws-stat-chip { background: rgba(255,255,255,0.04); border: 1px solid rgba(255,255,255,0.09); border-radius: 8px; padding: 12px 14px; }
    .ws-stat-label { font-size: 10px; text-transform: uppercase; letter-spacing: .06em; color: var(--text-secondary); opacity: .7; margin-bottom: 5px; }
    .ws-stat-value { font-size: 22px; font-weight: 800; color: var(--text-primary); line-height: 1; margin-bottom: 4px; }
    .ws-stat-sub { font-size: 11px; color: var(--text-secondary); opacity: .65; }
    .ws-chart-wrap { background: rgba(0,0,0,0.22); border-radius: 8px; padding: 14px; margin-bottom: 18px; border: 1px solid rgba(255,255,255,0.07); }
    .ws-interp { background: rgba(99,102,241,0.08); border: 1px solid rgba(99,102,241,0.22); border-radius: 8px; padding: 14px 16px; margin-bottom: 4px; }
    .ws-interp-title { font-size: 11px; font-weight: 700; text-transform: uppercase; letter-spacing: .07em; color: rgba(165,180,252,0.8); margin: 0 0 10px; }
    .ws-interp-item { font-size: 13px; color: var(--text-secondary); margin: 6px 0; line-height: 1.5; }
    /* Vendor diagnostic */
    .ws-diag-list { display: flex; flex-direction: column; gap: 9px; margin-bottom: 20px; }
    .ws-diag-row { display: flex; gap: 12px; padding: 11px 13px; background: rgba(255,255,255,0.03); border-radius: 7px; border: 1px solid rgba(255,255,255,0.07); }
    .ws-diag-num { font-size: 12px; font-weight: 700; color: rgba(99,102,241,0.7); min-width: 18px; padding-top: 2px; }
    .ws-diag-body { flex: 1; min-width: 0; }
    .ws-diag-q { font-size: 13px; color: var(--text-primary); margin-bottom: 8px; line-height: 1.45; }
    .ws-radio-row { display: flex; gap: 12px; margin-bottom: 8px; flex-wrap: wrap; }
    .ws-radio-label { display: flex; align-items: center; gap: 5px; cursor: pointer; }
    .ws-radio { accent-color: rgba(99,102,241,0.9); cursor: pointer; }
    .ws-radio-opt { font-size: 12px; font-weight: 600; padding: 2px 8px; border-radius: 4px; }
    .ws-radio-yes   { color: rgba(52,211,153,0.9); }
    .ws-radio-partly { color: rgba(251,191,36,0.9); }
    .ws-radio-no    { color: rgba(251,113,133,0.9); }

<div class="docs-tab-content active" id="sect-introduction"><div class="docs-chapter-header"><span class="docs-chapter-eyebrow">INTRODUCTION</span><h2 class="docs-chapter-title">Introduction</h2><span class="docs-chapter-accent"></span></div><div class="docs-markdown"><h2>Introduction</h2>
<p>The most important change in security operations is not that AI is entering the SOC. It is that the tiered analyst model that defined the SOC for the last two decades is beginning to cease functioning as the governing architecture of the operation.</p>
<p>That is a different claim from the usual market story. The usual story says that AI improves the SOC: it makes analysts faster, triage smarter, detection more efficient, and workflows more automated. This book makes a more specific and more consequential argument. It argues that enterprise security operations is undergoing <strong>architectural substitution</strong>, not feature evolution. The operating model built around alert queues, analyst tiers, manual escalations, and playbook-mediated response is being replaced by a new control system built around continuous sensing, machine reasoning, bounded agent execution, runtime governance, and a shared operational intelligence spine.</p>
<p>At first glance, that can sound like rhetoric. It is not. The shift is already measurable. Enterprises operating at what this framework calls <strong>Stage 2</strong> are eliminating large portions of L1 and L2 workload from production security operations today. They are not merely enriching analysts with copilots. They are relocating more of the operating burden into systems that sense continuously, reason across evidence, act within governed bounds, and generate auditable decision chains. The practical implication is stark: products designed primarily to improve the old tier model are not simply at risk of margin compression. Many are at risk of becoming architecturally unnecessary.</p>
<p>This is why the distinction between decline and substitution matters. A declining model can often be optimized, stretched, or defended through incremental improvement. A substituted model can survive for a while in installed bases, but it stops governing the future. The question for security leaders, product leaders, architects, and investors is therefore not whether AI will “change the SOC.” The real question is which products, teams, and design assumptions still belong to a tiered operating system—and which belong to the one replacing it.</p>
<p>This book offers a framework for answering that question.</p>
<hr />
<h2>Why this book exists now</h2>
<p>Security operations has lived for years inside a deceptively stable abstraction. Alerts arrive. Analysts triage. More complex cases escalate. Humans investigate. Playbooks assist. Managers measure throughput, response time, and detection performance. Entire product categories, buying patterns, role definitions, and service models have been built around that sequence.</p>
<p>But the sequence is now breaking for structural reasons.</p>
<p>First, the unit of work is changing. In a tiered SOC, the atomic unit is often the alert or ticket. In an agentic operating model, the atomic unit becomes the <strong>signal</strong>, the <strong>hypothesis</strong>, the <strong>authority-bounded action</strong>, and the <strong>evidence chain</strong> that connects them. That shift changes what the system must produce and what humans are for.</p>
<p>Second, the control surface is changing. In the old model, control is spread across staffing patterns, runbooks, approval layers, and tribal expertise. In the new model, control increasingly resides in machine-interpretable governance, authority scope, reasoning quality, and the integrity of the shared operational model.</p>
<p>Third, the sources of strategic advantage are changing. In a tiered world, value often accumulates around workflow convenience, analyst throughput, alert consolidation, or specialized human services. In the emerging model, value increasingly accumulates around reasoning depth, graph contribution, governance architecture, and integration into the live cybernetic loop of the operation.</p>
<p>These shifts are no longer speculative. They are visible in leading enterprise programs, in product roadmaps, in buyer evaluation criteria, and in the growing gap between tools that assist an old architecture and platforms that help construct a new one.</p>
<p>This book exists because that gap needs a vocabulary.</p>
<hr />
<h2>What ASAF is</h2>
<p>ASAF stands for the <strong>Agentic Security Operations Adoption Framework</strong>. It is a staging and evaluation model for understanding how security operations moves from the traditional SOC to a governed, agent-orchestrated control system.</p>
<p>The framework has four core parts:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>six maturity stages</strong>, from Traditional operations to fully agentic operations</li>
<li><strong>three operating planes</strong> — Sensing, Reasoning, and Control — which replace the old L1/L2/L3 mental model</li>
<li><strong>eleven dimensions</strong>, which define the full capability surface of the new architecture</li>
<li><strong>eight principles</strong>, which define the non-negotiable operating assumptions of an agentic security system</li>
</ul>
<p>ASAF is designed to do three things at once.</p>
<p>First, it helps leaders describe the transition with precision. Instead of talking vaguely about “AI-enabled SOC transformation,” it gives a reader a way to name what is changing, where a product sits, which capabilities matter most, and what stage an enterprise has actually reached.</p>
<p>Second, it helps buyers and architects evaluate platforms. It distinguishes between products that enable stage advancement, products that remain useful but non-structural, and products whose value proposition depends on unresolved Stage 0 and Stage 1 problems.</p>
<p>Third, it helps the market see that the future of security operations is not an analyst workflow with smarter tools attached. It is a new control system.</p>
<hr />
<h2>The shape of the replacement</h2>
<p>The cleanest way to understand the replacement architecture is to start with the three operating planes.</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Sensing</strong> replaces L1-style alert triage and initial classification with continuous, adversary-informed signal production.</li>
<li><strong>Reasoning</strong> replaces L2-style investigation with hypothesis-driven inference across a shared adversary and evidence model.</li>
<li><strong>Control</strong> replaces human-default escalation and playbook execution with bounded agent action governed by live authority constraints, policy, and traceability.</li>
</ul>
<p>These planes do not operate as isolated product categories. They function as a continuous loop. Signals feed reasoning. Reasoning directs execution. Execution writes outcomes into the shared operational model. Governance constrains and recalibrates all three. Human oversight increasingly governs intent, exception handling, and legitimacy rather than serving as the default processing layer for every alert.</p>
<p>This is why the tier metaphor breaks down. Tiers describe escalation layers in a human labor model. Planes describe signal-processing roles in a system architecture. Once the unit of analysis changes from analyst workload to system behavior, the old tier model stops clarifying what matters.</p>
<hr />
<h2>The stakes for vendors and buyers</h2>
<p>One of the most important consequences of this shift is that the market does not reorganize around “best features.” It reorganizes around <strong>architectural position</strong>.</p>
<p>ASAF groups vendors into three categories:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Enablers</strong> — products that accelerate stage advancement by contributing meaningfully to reasoning, execution, governance, or the shared intelligence spine</li>
<li><strong>Neutral players</strong> — products that remain useful in the environment but do not drive movement into the next operating model</li>
<li><strong>Displaced categories</strong> — products whose primary value depends on the tier model still being the organizing structure of the SOC</li>
</ul>
<p>This matters because many products that look competitive in a feature checklist become non-competitive once evaluated in architectural terms. A broad-feature product with shallow loop participation may be less strategically important than a narrower product that writes evidence into the graph, shapes governance, or materially improves reasoning quality.</p>
<p>For buyers, this means the most important question is not merely, “Does this tool work?” It is, “Does this tool belong in the system we are becoming?”</p>
<p>For vendors, the equivalent question is even tougher: “Are we helping the customer move into the next architecture, or are we monetizing friction inside the old one?”</p>
<hr />
<h2>Who this book is for</h2>
<p>This book is written for readers who need a strategic but operationally precise view of the transition.</p>
<p>It is especially for:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>CISOs and security leaders</strong> deciding where the operating model is headed and which categories are exposed</li>
<li><strong>security product leaders and platform builders</strong> deciding whether their products enable stage advancement or merely optimize legacy workflows</li>
<li><strong>platform architects and integration leaders</strong> designing how sensing, reasoning, execution, governance, and shared intelligence should fit together</li>
<li><strong>market strategists, investors, and GTM leaders</strong> trying to distinguish structural winners from temporary feature leaders</li>
</ul>
<p>You do not need to agree with every implication of the framework to use the book. But you do need to entertain its central premise: that the future of security operations is governed less by human tiering and more by the design of a machine-mediated control loop.</p>
<hr />
<h2>How to read this book</h2>
<p>This book is meant to be read front to back, because its argument accumulates.</p>
<p>The introduction establishes the burning platform and the shape of the framework. <strong>Chapter 1</strong> then replaces the reader’s inherited mental model by showing why Sensing, Reasoning, and Control are better descriptors of the new architecture than L1, L2, and L3. From there, the book moves plane by plane and then into the structural dimensions that make the full system coherent.</p>
<p>The reading arc is intentional:</p>
<ol>
<li>first, understand why the old model is breaking</li>
<li>then understand the architecture that replaces it</li>
<li>then understand the dimensions that make the architecture operational</li>
<li>finally, understand how the whole system behaves as one cybernetic loop</li>
</ol>
<p>Readers looking for a specific entry point can still use the later appendices and role-based artifacts. But the main text is designed as a cumulative argument, not a detached reference set.</p>
<hr />
<h2>What this book argues</h2>
<p>This book makes five claims.</p>
<ol>
<li>The tiered SOC is no longer the correct organizing abstraction for advanced security operations.</li>
<li>The replacement model is architectural, not cosmetic.</li>
<li>The transition can be staged, assessed, and compared.</li>
<li>Governance, reasoning, and graph contribution are becoming structurally decisive.</li>
<li>Vendor categories will increasingly be defined by integration depth in the loop, not by feature breadth in isolation.</li>
</ol>
<p>If those claims are right, then the future of security operations will not be determined by who best supports the old human workflow. It will be determined by who best helps enterprises build a governed system that can sense, reason, act, and prove what it did.</p>
<p>That is the argument this book will now build.</p>
<hr />
<h2>Three takeaways</h2>
<ul>
<li>The central shift is not “AI in the SOC,” but the end of the tiered SOC as the governing architecture.</li>
<li>ASAF provides a way to stage, assess, and compare that transition with more precision than generic transformation language allows.</li>
<li>The rest of the book explains the replacement model as a continuous argument, beginning with the three operating planes that displace the tier metaphor.</li>
</ul>
<h2>Two implications</h2>
<ul>
<li>Buyers should evaluate tools not just by utility, but by whether they belong in the architecture that is replacing the old model.</li>
<li>Vendors should assume that products monetizing unresolved tier-model friction are structurally exposed as enterprises advance beyond Stage 1.</li>
</ul>
<h2>Bridge to Chapter 1</h2>
<p>If the tiered SOC is ending, the next question is not which tool wins inside the old structure. It is what architectural model replaces L1, L2, and L3—and why that model better describes the future of security operations.</p></div></div>

<p><strong>Working Draft — Agentic SOC Architecture Framework (ASAF) | Framework Reference</strong></p>
<hr />
<h2>Why a Foundation Section Exists</h2>
<p>Every operational framework carries assumptions. ASAF carries several: that autonomy is better structured as a continuum than a switch; that ethics belongs inside the control loop, not above it; that human roles evolve rather than disappear. These assumptions do not belong buried inside dimension chapters. They shape how everything else in this framework should be read.</p>
<p>This section does three things. It maps the six maturity stages — what they mean, what separates them, and what realistic adoption looks like. It states the eight governing principles — the architectural commitments that distinguish ASAF from a collection of best practices. And it shows how those principles connect across the eleven dimensions that form the framework's operational logic.</p>
<hr />
<h2>Part One: The Six Maturity Stages</h2>
<p>The ASAF maturity model describes a transformation in how security operations are structured — from alert-queue processing by human analysts to a self-regulating autonomous control system governed by humans. The six stages are not milestones on a project plan. They are structural configurations, each with a characteristic operational posture, human role model, and governance approach.</p>
<p>Most large enterprises in 2025 sit at Stage 0 or 1. A small number have begun Stage 2 transitions. Stage 3 is the credible near-term target for advanced security programs over the next three to five years.</p>
<hr />
<h3>Stage 0 — Traditional (Tiered SOC)</h3>
<p>The classic L1/L2/L3 analyst model that has defined enterprise security operations since the early 2000s. Operations are alert-driven and reactive. Human analysts process queues, follow runbooks, and escalate according to tier boundaries. SIEM and SOAR are the primary tools. Governance lives in policy documents that are reviewed episodically.</p>
<p><strong>Autonomy level:</strong> None. Humans execute every detection, triage, investigation, and response action.</p>
<p><strong>Human model:</strong> Tiered analysts with senior analysts as escalation endpoints and managers as approvers.</p>
<p><strong>Governance model:</strong> Static policy documents. Periodic compliance reviews. No real-time enforcement.</p>
<p><strong>Detection posture:</strong> Alert-queue processing. Signature and rule-based detection. SIEM correlation as the primary aggregation layer.</p>
<p><strong>Knowledge model:</strong> Tribal knowledge, runbooks, and unstructured wikis. No structured operational knowledge graph.</p>
<p><strong>Characteristic failure mode:</strong> Alert fatigue and throughput bottlenecks drive hiring cycles without improving detection quality. The system scales human cost faster than it scales detection capability.</p>
<p><em>Approximate timeline: Dominant model from 2020 to 2024.</em></p>
<hr />
<h3>Stage 1 — Assisted (AI-Augmented)</h3>
<p>AI and automation assist analysts with triage, enrichment, and playbook execution. Humans still own all decisions. Automation reduces mean-time-to-respond for known threat patterns. Alert fatigue begins to be addressed — but the tier model remains structurally intact.</p>
<p><strong>Autonomy level:</strong> Low. Automation executes pre-approved playbooks. Humans approve all significant actions.</p>
<p><strong>Human model:</strong> Tiered analysts assisted by automation. Senior analysts focus on complex investigations.</p>
<p><strong>Governance model:</strong> Policy codified in playbooks. Automated compliance checks on known scenarios. Policy remains document-centric.</p>
<p><strong>Detection posture:</strong> ML-assisted prioritization. Behavioral anomaly detection augmenting signature rules.</p>
<p><strong>Knowledge model:</strong> Structured runbooks. Case management with enrichment. Basic threat intelligence integration.</p>
<p><strong>Characteristic failure mode:</strong> Automation debt. Playbooks proliferate without governance or maintenance. False positive rates are suppressed rather than solved.</p>
<p><em>Approximate timeline: Dominant model from 2024 to 2025.</em></p>
<hr />
<h3>Stage 2 — Supervised Autonomy (Agents with Approval Gates)</h3>
<p>Agents execute bounded, pre-authorized investigation and response tasks autonomously. Humans approve significant actions through intent-based authorization. The tier model weakens as agents absorb L1 and L2 workloads.</p>
<p><strong>Autonomy level:</strong> Moderate. Agents autonomously investigate and contain within pre-authorized scope. Humans approve scope-expanding actions.</p>
<p><strong>Human model:</strong> Analysts become agent supervisors. Role identity shifts from throughput execution to oversight and exception handling.</p>
<p><strong>Governance model:</strong> Governance rules embedded in agent execution frameworks. Authority scope defined per agent class. Policy begins to become machine-interpretable.</p>
<p><strong>Detection posture:</strong> Agent-driven detection hypotheses. Continuous signal fusion. CTEM integration begins.</p>
<p><strong>Knowledge model:</strong> Security Knowledge Graph prototype. Policy and evidence begin to link. Adversary model is tracked.</p>
<p><strong>Characteristic failure mode:</strong> Governance theater — authority boundaries defined in documents but not technically enforced. The tier model persists in behavior even as titles change.</p>
<p><em>Approximate timeline: Leading-edge programs from 2025 to 2026.</em></p>
<hr />
<h3>Stage 3 — Directed Autonomy (Intent-Driven Operations)</h3>
<p>Humans define operational intent, scope constraints, and ethical boundaries. Agents plan, reason, and execute autonomously within those bounds. Escalation is replaced by bounded exception handling. The tier model is fully eliminated.</p>
<p><strong>Autonomy level:</strong> High. Agents plan multi-step investigation and response chains. Humans define scope and handle genuine novelty.</p>
<p><strong>Human model:</strong> Post-tier roles emerge: Security Architects define scope and intent. Response Authorities approve novel actions. Governance Officers maintain ethical bounds.</p>
<p><strong>Governance model:</strong> Machine-interpretable policy. An ethics engine runs as an operational control loop. Authority is modeled in the knowledge graph.</p>
<p><strong>Detection posture:</strong> Competing hypothesis model. Continuous pre-emptive and reactive operations. Exposure-driven prioritization is the primary operational model.</p>
<p><strong>Knowledge model:</strong> Active Security Knowledge Graph. Governance, confidence, and adversary entities are first-class nodes.</p>
<p><strong>Characteristic failure mode:</strong> Governance engine gaps — ethics and authority modeled incompletely, with edge cases exposed in incidents. Human role identity crisis as governance roles feel less valued than operational roles.</p>
<p><em>Approximate timeline: Advanced programs from 2026 to 2027.</em></p>
<hr />
<h3>Stage 4 — Collaborative Agentic (Agent-First with Human Governance)</h3>
<p>Agent-first operations across all security functions. Humans govern legitimacy, ethics, and organizational intent. Agents coordinate, compete, and resolve conflicts autonomously. DFIR, threat research, and exposure management are continuous functions — not projects.</p>
<p><strong>Autonomy level:</strong> Very high. Agents handle all operational execution. Humans maintain governance authority and handle ethics-boundary decisions.</p>
<p><strong>Human model:</strong> Governance Officers hold ethical veto authority. Security Strategists define long-horizon intent. Assurance Officers validate agent behavior continuously.</p>
<p><strong>Governance model:</strong> Governance as a continuous operational signal. The ethics engine enforces proportionality, legality, and scope in real time.</p>
<p><strong>Detection posture:</strong> Fully continuous. CTEM, DFIR, threat research, and response are unified and simultaneously active.</p>
<p><strong>Knowledge model:</strong> Full SKG operational. The graph drives planning, reasoning, orchestration, and artifact generation.</p>
<p><strong>Characteristic failure mode:</strong> Governance overconfidence — governance officers trust the system without adequate oversight rigor. Vendor concentration limits constitutional authority.</p>
<p><em>Approximate timeline: Vanguard programs from 2027 to 2028.</em></p>
<hr />
<h3>Stage 5 — Fully Agentic (Autonomous Control System)</h3>
<p>Security Operations is a self-regulating autonomous control system. Agents continuously sense, reason, act, and learn across all security domains. Humans govern intent, audit outcomes, and hold constitutional authority over the system's ethical and legal boundaries.</p>
<p><strong>Autonomy level:</strong> Full. Agents operate the security control system. Humans govern the governing model itself.</p>
<p><strong>Human model:</strong> Constitutional Governance role defines system values and authority boundaries. Chief Trust Officer owns audit and legitimacy. Strategic Security Architect owns long-horizon system design.</p>
<p><strong>Governance model:</strong> Ethics and governance are part of the operating kernel. Every action is governed, logged, explainable, and revocable.</p>
<p><strong>Detection posture:</strong> Predictive and pre-emptive by default. Adversary modeling informs continuous exposure management and detection architecture.</p>
<p><strong>Knowledge model:</strong> The SKG is self-evolving. It continuously integrates threat intelligence, incident learning, and governance updates without human curation.</p>
<p><strong>Characteristic failure mode:</strong> Adversarial manipulation of governance boundaries. Adversaries probe authority models and attempt to exploit confidence thresholds. Constitutional resilience requires continuous red-team testing.</p>
<p><em>Approximate timeline: Theoretical horizon from 2028 to 2030.</em></p>
<hr />
<h2>What Stage Are You At?</h2>
<p>The ASAF Maturity Worksheet in the appendix provides a structured self-assessment across all eleven dimensions. Most enterprise programs find that their stage varies significantly by dimension — they may be at Stage 2 in agent execution while remaining at Stage 0 in knowledge graph architecture. That variance is the diagnostic signal. The lowest-scoring dimensions constrain the capability ceiling of the dimensions that score higher.</p>
<p>The most common stage distribution in 2025: Stage 1 across SEN and RSN, Stage 0 across GOV and OPS, Stage 0 to 1 across LRN and HUM.</p>
<hr />
<h2>Part Two: The Eight Governing Principles</h2>
<p>The governing principles are not aspirational statements. They are architectural commitments — choices about how the framework is structured that distinguish it from incremental process improvement. An organization can adopt ASAF's tools without adopting its principles. But if it does, it will build a more expensive version of what it already has.</p>
<p>Each principle is stated as a factual claim about how agentic security operations work at maturity. Disagreement with a principle is disagreement with the framework's premises, not disagreement with its implementation details.</p>
<hr />
<h3>P1 — Security Operations is a Cybernetic System</h3>
<blockquote>
<p>"Security Operations is a cybernetic system — a continuous feedback loop of sensing, reasoning, action, and learning — not a linear workflow of tiered human escalations."</p>
</blockquote>
<p>The cybernetic model is foundational. A cybernetic system maintains a desired state through continuous sensing and corrective action. A linear escalation model does not — it responds to threshold crossings, not continuous state divergence. The difference between these architectures is not a matter of tool selection. It is a matter of how the system is designed to behave when it encounters something it has not seen before.</p>
<p>ASAF's four primary dimensions — SEN, RSN, ACT, LRN — form the operational feedback loop. The remaining seven dimensions structure, govern, coordinate, and sustain it. But the loop is primary. Everything else serves the loop.</p>
<hr />
<h3>P2 — Governance is an Operational Control Signal</h3>
<blockquote>
<p>"Ethics, governance, and authority are operational control signals that shape every action in real time. They are not oversight layers applied after the fact."</p>
</blockquote>
<p>The most common failure mode in autonomous security systems is treating governance as an external audit function — a checkpoint that reviews what the system did. ASAF treats governance as a continuous constraint that shapes what the system can do. The GOV dimension does not sit above the operational loop. It sits inside it, as a real-time limiting function on every action the ACT and AGT dimensions can execute.</p>
<p>This principle has architectural consequences. Governance cannot be an API call to a compliance database. It must be machine-interpretable policy embedded in the authority model, evaluated on every action before it is executed.</p>
<hr />
<h3>P3 — Autonomy Must Be Bounded, Proportional, Explainable, and Revocable</h3>
<blockquote>
<p>"Autonomy must be scoped, proportional, explainable, auditable, and revocable. Unbounded autonomy is an architectural failure, not a capability goal."</p>
</blockquote>
<p>No mature security architecture pursues maximum autonomy. It pursues appropriate autonomy — the level of autonomous action that is both operationally effective and organizationally defensible. The boundary between appropriate and inappropriate autonomy shifts with organizational maturity, regulatory context, and incident history. The framework that makes that boundary explicit, technical, and adjustable is more valuable than the framework that maximizes agent capability.</p>
<p>Bounded autonomy is not a limitation on ASAF. It is a design goal.</p>
<hr />
<h3>P4 — Operations Are Continuous and Bidirectional</h3>
<blockquote>
<p>"Planning, detection, response, and learning operate continuously and bidirectionally. Every action feeds the knowledge model; every new signal may alter the operational plan."</p>
</blockquote>
<p>Sequential operations — detect, then investigate, then respond, then close — are efficient for known scenarios. They are brittle for unknown ones. Continuous bidirectional operations maintain parallel detection, investigation, and response threads simultaneously. A new signal does not wait for the previous response to close. It enters the system immediately, is reasoned about, and may generate new action threads before existing ones resolve.</p>
<p>This principle defines the OPS dimension's ambition: not faster escalation chains, but the structural elimination of the need for escalation chains.</p>
<hr />
<h3>P5 — Humans Govern Intent, Not Alert Queues</h3>
<blockquote>
<p>"Humans govern intent, scope, and legitimacy — not alert queues. Human value is derived from judgment, authority, and ethical accountability, not task throughput."</p>
</blockquote>
<p>This principle defines what "human in the loop" means in a mature agentic security operation. Humans are not in the loop to process more alerts. They are in the loop to define what the system is trying to accomplish, to set the ethical and legal boundaries within which it operates, and to hold accountability for its outcomes.</p>
<p>The shift from throughput work to governance work is not a reduction in human importance. It is an increase in the quality of human contribution. But it requires a different skill set, a different org chart, and a different relationship to the technology.</p>
<hr />
<h3>P6 — The Security Knowledge Graph is the Operational Spine</h3>
<blockquote>
<p>"The Security Knowledge Graph is the operational spine — connecting policy, evidence, adversary intelligence, confidence, authority, and audit artifacts as first-class entities."</p>
</blockquote>
<p>The SKG is not a SIEM replacement. It is not a threat intelligence platform. It is the shared data model through which all dimensions in the framework communicate. When an agent reasons about a threat, it reasons over the SKG. When governance evaluates an action, it queries the SKG. When learning updates detection, it updates the SKG. When an audit asks why an action was taken, the answer is in the SKG.</p>
<p>Without the SKG, ASAF's dimensions are well-designed components. With it, they are a coordinated system.</p>
<hr />
<h3>P7 — Operations Are Non-Linear</h3>
<blockquote>
<p>"Agentic operations do not follow linear kill-chain or escalation models. They operate as competing hypotheses, parallel investigations, and continuous exposure management."</p>
</blockquote>
<p>The kill chain model describes how adversaries operate. It has been incorrectly used as a model for how defenders should operate. Defenders who wait for the kill chain to progress before acting give adversaries time. Defenders who run competing hypotheses in parallel, investigate multiple threads simultaneously, and manage exposure continuously do not.</p>
<p>Non-linear operations require a different reasoning architecture (competing hypothesis evaluation, not sequential triage), a different operational model (concurrent threads, not queue processing), and a different knowledge substrate (graph-structured relationships, not flat case records).</p>
<hr />
<h3>P8 — Every Decision Must Be Traceable</h3>
<blockquote>
<p>"Every decision, action, and outcome must be traceable through the system to its authorizing scope, evidence chain, confidence level, and governance approval."</p>
</blockquote>
<p>Traceability is not an audit requirement imposed on the system. It is an operational requirement for operating autonomous systems responsibly. When an autonomous agent takes a consequential action — isolating a system, blocking an account, triggering a remediation — there must be a complete record of what evidence justified the action, what authority permitted it, what confidence threshold triggered it, and what governance rule allowed it to execute without human approval.</p>
<p>Traceability is how organizations maintain accountability for autonomous decisions. It is also how they improve the system: patterns in the traceability record reveal where confidence thresholds are miscalibrated, where governance boundaries are too narrow or too wide, and where detection quality is degrading.</p>
